title: == vs equals()
short: == compares primitive values or object references; equals() expresses logical equality.
answer: For primitives, == compares values; for object references, == checks whether both references refer to the same object. equals() is intended for logical equality and can be overridden by a class. If equals() is overridden, hashCode() must obey the contract that equal objects have equal hash codes, which is essential for HashMap and HashSet.
followups: Why must equals() and hashCode() agree?
What happens in HashSet if the contract is broken?
Why should equals() usually be symmetric and transitive?
interview: In an interview I distinguish identity from logical state. == answers “is it the same object?” while equals() answers “should these objects be considered equal?”. For hash-based collections, the equals/hashCode contract is critical.

title: equals() and hashCode() contract
short: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
answer: Hash-based collections use hashCode to locate a bucket and equals to confirm the key. Unequal objects may collide.
followups: What breaks if hashCode is omitted?
interview: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

title: HashMap internal working
short: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.
answer: HashMap spreads the hash, maps it to a bucket and handles collisions. Modern Java can treeify heavily-collided buckets under suitable conditions. Resize redistributes entries.
interview: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
short: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.
answer: ArrayList is usually the better default. LinkedList has O(n) indexed access and only helps for specific operations/access patterns.
followups: Which is better for random access?
interview: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.

title: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet
short: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.
answer: Hash-based sets usually provide expected O(1) basic operations. TreeSet is generally O(log n).
interview: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.

title: How to create an immutable class
short: Prevent observable state changes after construction.
answer: Use private final fields, constructor initialization, no setters, defensive copies and final class where appropriate.
code: public final class User { private final String name; public User(String n){name=n;} }
interview: Prevent observable state changes after construction.

title: final vs finally vs finalize
short: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.
answer: final restricts reassignment/overriding/inheritance. finally normally executes after try/catch. Do not rely on finalize for cleanup.
interview: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.

title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions
short: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.
answer: Choose based on whether callers can reasonably recover and where errors are translated.
interview: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.

title: Try-with-resources
short: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.
answer: Resources close even when exceptions occur; close failures can be represented as suppressed exceptions.
interview: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.

title: Abstract class vs interface
short: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.
answer: Use abstract classes for genuine shared base behavior/state and interfaces for capabilities/contracts.
code:
interface Auditable{void audit();}
abstract class Base{Long id;}
interview: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.

title: Default and static interface methods
short: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.
answer: Default methods help evolve interfaces. Static interface methods are called through the interface name and are not instance overrides.
code: interface Loggable { default void log(){} static String level(){return "INFO";} }
interview: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.

title: Optional usage
short: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.
answer: It is particularly useful for return types. It should not automatically replace null in every field or parameter.
interview: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.

title: Functional interface
short: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.
answer: It can be targeted by lambdas/method references. Default and static methods do not count.
interview: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.

title: Lambda expression
short: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.
answer: Types are inferred from the target type. Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
interview: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.

title: Record
short: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.
answer: Records are final with final component references, but referenced objects can still be mutable.
interview: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.

title: Virtual threads
short: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.
answer: They make thread-per-task models practical at large concurrency. They do not make CPU work intrinsically faster.
interview: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.

title: synchronized
short: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.
answer: Only one thread holds a monitor at a time. Synchronization also establishes happens-before relationships.
interview: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.

title: volatile vs AtomicInteger
short: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.
answer: volatile does not make count++ atomic. AtomicInteger supports increment and compare-and-set style operations.
interview: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.

title: Deadlock and prevention
short: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.
answer: Prevent with consistent lock ordering, small lock scopes, avoiding nested locks and timed acquisition where appropriate.
interview: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.

title: Heap vs stack
short: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.
answer: Heap is shared and GC-managed. A stack holds method frames and local execution state.
interview: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.

title: Garbage collection
short: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.
answer: Collectors trade throughput, latency and memory footprint. Allocation rate and retention still matter.
interview: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.

title: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
short: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized.
answer: String is immutable, so repeated concatenation creates new String objects. StringBuilder is mutable and is the usual choice for single-threaded iterative construction. StringBuffer provides similar mutable operations but synchronizes its methods, so it is generally slower and is only useful when that legacy synchronization requirement matters. In modern concurrent code, explicit synchronization or other concurrency primitives are usually preferable.
followups: What is the time complexity of repeated String concatenation in a loop?
interview: For loops that build text repeatedly, I use StringBuilder because it avoids creating a new String for every append. I choose StringBuffer only when I specifically need its synchronized API; otherwise StringBuilder is the simpler and faster default.

title: Comparable vs Comparator
short: Comparable defines natural order; Comparator defines external ordering.
answer: Comparable defines a class’s natural ordering through compareTo(). Comparator defines an external ordering through compare(), so the same class can have multiple sorting strategies without changing the domain class. Comparable is useful when one ordering is intrinsic; Comparator is better for contextual choices such as sorting employees by salary, name, or joining date.
followups: Can a class implement multiple Comparables?
How do you sort by salary and then name?
What happens when compareTo returns zero?
interview: I use Comparable when the object has one obvious natural order. I use Comparator when sorting requirements vary or when I cannot modify the class. In Java streams and collections, Comparator also composes well with comparing(), thenComparing(), reversed(), and null handling.

title: map vs flatMap
short: map is one-to-one transformation; flatMap transforms and flattens nested streams.
answer: map transforms each stream element into exactly one result, while flatMap transforms each element into a stream and then flattens all those streams into one stream. A common example is converting List<List<String>> into Stream<String>. flatMap is therefore useful for one-to-many relationships, nested collections, and optional/stream composition.
followups: What is the difference between Optional.map and Optional.flatMap?
Can flatMap change the number of elements?
interview: The key question I ask is whether the transformation produces one value or multiple values. If it is one-to-one, I use map; if it produces a collection or stream that must be flattened, I use flatMap.

title: parallelStream
short: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.
answer: It can help sufficiently large CPU-bound independent work and hurt for blocking I/O/shared state/small data.
interview: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.

title: Class loading in JVM
short: The JVM loads, links and initializes classes as needed.
answer: Loading finds bytecode; linking verifies/prepares/resolves; initialization runs class initialization when required.
interview: The JVM loads, links and initializes classes as needed.

title: Java memory leak
short: Reachable objects that should have been released can still consume heap.
answer: Common causes include static collections, unbounded caches, listeners and ThreadLocal misuse.
interview: Reachable objects that should have been released can still consume heap.

title: ThreadLocal risks
short: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, which can be risky in pooled threads.
answer: Remove values in finally where appropriate. ThreadLocal does not automatically propagate across executor threads.
interview: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, which can be risky in pooled threads.

title: CompletableFuture
short: It represents a future result and supports asynchronous composition.
answer: thenApply transforms, thenCompose flattens dependent futures and allOf combines work.
interview: It represents a future result and supports asynchronous composition.

title: ExecutorService vs ForkJoinPool
short: ExecutorService is general; ForkJoinPool is optimized for work stealing.
answer: Choose based on workload and isolation; blocking I/O should not casually share a CPU-oriented common pool.
interview: ExecutorService is general; ForkJoinPool is optimized for work stealing.

title: Why is String immutable in Java?
short: String cannot be changed after creation; operations create new String values.
answer: Immutability makes String safe to share, enables string pooling, simplifies caching and hashing, and avoids surprising changes when a String is used as a map key. Its internal representation is private and String does not expose mutating operations.
followups: Why is String a good HashMap key?
mistakes: Saying concat changes the original String.
Assuming immutability means no new objects are created.
interview: String is immutable, which makes it safe to share and hash, supports the string pool, and prevents a caller from changing a value after it has been passed around.

title: Explain the String pool.
short: The JVM maintains a pool of canonical String literals so identical literals can share storage.
answer: A literal such as "java" is normally interned in the String pool. If the same literal appears again, the references can point to the same pooled object. new String("java") creates a distinct object, while intern() returns the pooled representation.
followups: Where is the String pool located in modern JVMs?
Why should == not be used for String content?
mistakes: Treating all Strings as pooled.
Using == instead of equals() for content comparison.
interview: The String pool stores canonical representations of literals. It reduces duplicate literal objects, but explicitly created Strings can still live outside the pool.

title: What is defensive copying?
short: Defensive copying protects mutable internal state by copying objects at boundaries.
answer: If a class stores a mutable List or Date supplied by a caller, the caller could otherwise mutate the class state. A defensive copy is made on input and often again on output. For modern Java, immutable collections can also help when the data itself is immutable.
followups: Why is returning the internal list dangerous?
mistakes: Only copying on construction but exposing the internal list.
Assuming an unmodifiable view always makes the underlying data immutable.
interview: Defensive copying prevents external code from changing internal mutable state. I use copies or immutable collections at API boundaries.

title: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
short: A shallow copy copies the outer object while nested references remain shared; a deep copy also duplicates the nested mutable state.
answer: For an object containing a mutable Address, a shallow copy can leave both objects pointing to the same Address. Mutating that Address then affects both copies. Deep copying duplicates the object graph that must be independently mutable.
followups: How would you deep copy safely?
Why can serialization-based copying be problematic?
mistakes: Calling clone() a universal deep-copy solution.
Ignoring cycles and shared references in object graphs.
interview: Shallow copy duplicates the outer object; deep copy duplicates the mutable nested state that should not be shared.

title: Explain covariant return types.
short: An overriding method can return a subtype of the return type declared by the parent method.
answer: Java allows an overriding method to narrow the return type covariantly. This improves usability because callers of the subclass can receive the more specific type without an explicit cast.
followups: Can parameters be narrowed when overriding?
How is covariance different from method overloading?
mistakes: Calling contravariant parameter changes valid overriding.
Confusing overload resolution with overriding.
interview: Covariant returns let an overriding method return a more specific subtype while preserving the parent contract.

title: What is the Java Memory Model?
short: The Java Memory Model defines how threads interact through memory and what visibility and ordering guarantees synchronization constructs provide.
answer: The JMM explains happens-before relationships. synchronized, volatile, final-field guarantees and concurrent utilities establish visibility and ordering rules. Without a happens-before relationship, one thread is not guaranteed to observe another thread's writes in the expected order.
mistakes: Saying volatile makes compound operations atomic.
Assuming CPU cache behavior alone defines Java semantics.
interview: The JMM gives Java its visibility and ordering rules across threads. I reason about shared state using happens-before rather than relying on timing or CPU behavior.

title: Why is i++ not atomic?
short: Increment consists of read, modify and write operations, so multiple threads can lose updates.
answer: For a shared int, i++ can read the same old value in two threads and both write the same incremented result. AtomicInteger provides an atomic increment operation using concurrency primitives.
mistakes: Calling i++ atomic because int reads/writes are atomic.
Using AtomicInteger without considering the larger invariant.
interview: i++ is a read-modify-write sequence, not one atomic action. AtomicInteger or locking is needed when multiple threads update shared state.

title: When should you use AtomicInteger versus synchronized?
short: AtomicInteger is useful for independent atomic state updates; synchronized is better when multiple variables or invariants must change together.
answer: Atomic classes provide lock-free-style atomic operations for specific state transitions. If a business operation requires checking and updating several fields consistently, a synchronized block or Lock can protect the whole invariant.
followups: Can multiple atomic variables replace a lock for every design?
mistakes: Choosing atomics for a multi-field invariant.
Assuming atomic means globally thread-safe for surrounding business logic.
interview: I use atomics for simple independent counters or state transitions. For a compound invariant, I prefer a lock around the whole critical section.

title: What is ThreadLocal and when can it be dangerous?
short: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own value, but values can leak across reused thread-pool threads if not removed.
answer: ThreadLocal is useful for request-scoped context in synchronous code, but application servers reuse worker threads. If a large object or security context remains attached, it can survive beyond the request. Call remove() in cleanup code when appropriate.
followups: Does ThreadLocal work across async thread switches?
Why are virtual threads different for ThreadLocal usage?
mistakes: Treating ThreadLocal as global storage.
Forgetting cleanup with thread pools.
interview: ThreadLocal isolates values per thread, but pooled threads live for many requests, so I always consider lifecycle and cleanup.

title: What are virtual threads in Java 21?
short: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads designed for high-concurrency blocking workloads.
answer: A virtual thread is cheap compared with a platform thread and can be parked when it blocks, allowing the JVM to reuse carrier threads. They are especially useful for request-per-task applications that perform blocking I/O. They do not make CPU-bound work faster.
followups: Should CPU-bound work use virtual threads?
mistakes: Saying virtual threads are faster CPU threads.
Creating unbounded external resources simply because threads are cheap.
interview: Virtual threads improve scalability for large numbers of mostly blocking tasks. They reduce thread-management cost but do not remove CPU, database or downstream bottlenecks.

title: What is try-with-resources?
short: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources when leaving the try block, including when an exception occurs.
answer: The compiler generates cleanup logic around resources declared in the try header. If both the body and close operation throw, the close exception can become a suppressed exception.
followups: What interface must a resource implement?
mistakes: Manually closing resources in a finally block when try-with-resources is clearer.
Ignoring close failures completely.
interview: try-with-resources gives deterministic cleanup for AutoCloseable resources and correctly handles exceptional paths and suppressed exceptions.

title: Diagnose a Java memory leak in production
short: Use heap evidence and GC behavior to distinguish retained objects from high allocation.
answer: Compare post-GC heap trends, capture a heap dump, inspect dominators and GC roots, then identify the retaining path. Common causes include unbounded caches, static collections, listeners, ThreadLocals and long-lived executors. Validate the fix with the same workload.
followups: How do you investigate native memory?
mistakes: Assuming every OOM is a heap leak.
interview: I first prove retention after GC, then use a heap dump and GC roots to find who is keeping the objects alive. I fix the owner and verify post-GC usage stabilizes.

title: Explain Java Memory Model and happens-before
short: The JMM defines visibility and ordering between threads; happens-before gives a guarantee that one action is visible before another.
answer: Locks, volatile writes/reads, thread start/join and concurrent utilities establish happens-before relationships. Without them, compiler and CPU reordering means another thread is not guaranteed to observe a write when expected.
followups: Why is volatile not enough for i++?
mistakes: Saying volatile makes every operation atomic.
interview: I use JMM-defined happens-before relationships instead of timing assumptions. Volatile gives visibility and ordering for the variable, but not atomicity for compound operations.

title: When would you use Atomic classes or VarHandle?
short: Use them for narrow atomic state transitions where lock-free coordination is justified.
answer: Atomic classes provide common CAS operations; VarHandle exposes lower-level memory access modes. They work well for independent counters and state machines, while locks are often clearer for multi-field invariants.
followups: When can lock-free code be slower?
mistakes: Assuming lock-free always means faster.
interview: I choose the simplest correct primitive. Atomics are excellent for independent state; synchronized or Lock is preferable when several values must change together.

title: Explain virtual threads for backend services
short: Virtual threads make large numbers of blocking I/O tasks cheap to park, but do not increase CPU capacity or database capacity.
answer: They are scheduled on carrier threads and are useful for request-per-task workloads. You still need bounded downstream resources, connection pools and backpressure because cheap concurrency can overwhelm dependencies.
followups: When would reactive programming still help?
mistakes: Treating virtual threads as unlimited throughput.
interview: I would use virtual threads for I/O-heavy blocking workloads while still limiting DB connections and downstream concurrency.

title: How do you diagnose CPU spikes in Java?
short: Correlate CPU, thread state, GC and code-level profiles during the spike.
answer: Use JFR or async-profiler, thread dumps and GC logs. Check hot methods, serialization, regex, logging, busy loops, GC CPU and traffic changes. Compare with a healthy period.
followups: How do you distinguish lock contention from CPU work?
What does a thread dump show?
mistakes: Changing JVM settings before profiling.
interview: I first establish whether CPU is application code, GC or JVM overhead. Then I profile during the incident and fix the measured hotspot.

title: How do you prevent ThreadLocal leaks?
short: Clear request-specific ThreadLocal state when pooled tasks finish.
answer: ThreadLocal values belong to worker threads, which live much longer than requests. Always remove context in finally blocks and be careful when crossing executor boundaries.
followups: Does ThreadLocal propagate to async tasks?
mistakes: Assuming ThreadLocal follows tasks automatically.
interview: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, not request-scoped. In pools I always clean it up to prevent memory retention and context leakage.

title: How would you investigate a Java deadlock?
short: Use thread dumps to identify the circular wait and then fix lock ordering or ownership.
answer: Look for BLOCKED threads, lock owners and cycles. Multiple dumps help confirm the condition. Durable fixes include consistent acquisition order, smaller critical sections or redesigning shared state.
mistakes: Looking only at CPU usage.
interview: I map the lock ownership cycle from a thread dump back to code, then remove the circular dependency rather than relying on a restart.

title: How do you safely publish immutable Java state?
short: Construct it fully, use final fields and publish the reference through a JMM-safe mechanism.
answer: Final fields protect construction semantics; volatile, synchronization, concurrent collections or static initialization can establish visibility of the reference. Mutable inputs should be defensively copied.
code:
private volatile Config config;
void publish(Config c) { config = c; }
followups: Can an immutable object be unsafely published?
mistakes: Assuming immutability alone guarantees visibility.
interview: I combine immutability with safe publication. Immutability removes mutation races, while safe publication guarantees other threads see the intended state.

title: How do you tune Java performance scientifically?
short: Profile first, change one bottleneck, and compare against a reproducible baseline.
answer: Correlate throughput and p99 latency with CPU, allocation, GC, locks, DB and downstream latency. Use JFR, async-profiler and load tests. Avoid tuning from folklore.
code: // Baseline -> profile -> targeted change -> same workload -> compare p99.
mistakes: Changing heap/GC settings without evidence.
interview: I do not tune the JVM blindly. I establish a baseline, identify the dominant bottleneck, make one change and verify it under the same workload.

title: Explain ForkJoinPool work stealing
short: Workers use local deques and steal tasks from other workers when idle, making it effective for CPU-bound fork/join work.
answer: Blocking I/O can occupy workers and reduce effective parallelism. Dedicated executors are safer for blocking workloads.
followups: How does CompletableFuture choose an executor?
How do you isolate blocking calls?
mistakes: Using the common pool for blocking database calls.
interview: ForkJoinPool is optimized for parallel CPU work. I avoid unbounded blocking operations in the common pool because they can starve unrelated tasks.

title: What is false sharing?
short: Independent hot variables on the same CPU cache line can cause unnecessary cache invalidation between cores.
answer: It matters mainly in highly concurrent low-latency code. Padding or layout annotations can help, but only after measurement with a benchmark or profiler.
code: // Validate with JMH before introducing padding.
mistakes: Adding padding without evidence.
interview: I treat false sharing as a measured hardware-level optimization, not a default design rule.

title: CPU usage spikes after switching to parallel streams
short: Parallel streams can increase throughput for suitable CPU-bound workloads, but they also consume shared executor capacity.
answer: I would profile CPU and common-pool contention first. If the workload is already concurrent or too small, sequential processing may be faster. For isolated batch work I would use a dedicated executor with controlled parallelism.
code: Remove parallelism if the workload is small or already concurrent. For controlled background workloads, use an appropriately sized executor instead of allowing common-pool work to compete with unrelated tasks.
followups: How does the common ForkJoinPool work?
How do virtual threads differ from parallel streams?
mistakes: Using parallel streams for blocking I/O.
Assuming more parallelism always means more throughput.
interview: I would not assume parallelStream is automatically faster. I would benchmark it and check whether it competes with other workloads for the common pool.
scenario: A batch endpoint uses parallelStream() and production CPU reaches 100%, while unrelated requests become slower.
investigation: Inspect ForkJoinPool activity, CPU profiles and request concurrency. Determine whether the work is CPU-bound and whether parallelism is competing with request threads.
resolution: Remove parallelism if the workload is small or already concurrent. For controlled background workloads, use an appropriately sized executor instead of allowing common-pool work to compete with unrelated tasks.
prevention: Benchmark realistic data sizes and concurrency. Treat the common ForkJoinPool as shared infrastructure rather than a free worker pool.

title: ThreadLocal data leaks between requests in a pooled executor
short: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, not request-scoped; pooled threads survive after a request finishes.
answer: I would always clear ThreadLocal state in a finally block when using it with thread pools. For modern applications I would consider explicit context objects or framework-supported context propagation instead.
code: Use try/finally to remove ThreadLocal values, or prefer explicit context propagation mechanisms. Avoid storing large request objects in ThreadLocal.
followups: Why can ThreadLocal cause memory leaks?
How does this interact with virtual threads?
mistakes: Setting ThreadLocal without remove().
Assuming a pooled thread is destroyed after each request.
interview: ThreadLocal is safe only when its lifecycle matches the thread. In a pool, that means I must clean it after every task.
scenario: A request stores user context in ThreadLocal. A later request handled by the same pooled thread unexpectedly sees the previous request’s value.
investigation: Inspect where ThreadLocal is set and removed. Confirm thread reuse and whether exceptions can bypass cleanup.
resolution: Use try/finally to remove ThreadLocal values, or prefer explicit context propagation mechanisms. Avoid storing large request objects in ThreadLocal.
prevention: Add tests for thread reuse and monitor memory retention. Keep request context scoped and cleaned deterministically.

title: A synchronized section becomes a throughput bottleneck
short: Synchronization provides correctness but can serialize throughput when a hot shared lock protects too much work.
answer: I would profile lock contention, minimize the critical section and look for key-based partitioning. If the access pattern fits, ConcurrentHashMap or finer-grained synchronization can improve concurrency.
code: Reduce the critical section, use concurrent data structures where appropriate and partition state by key so independent operations do not share one lock. Do not replace synchronized with another lock without measuring.
mistakes: Removing synchronization without proving thread safety.
Holding a lock while performing remote I/O.
interview: The question is not whether synchronized is slow; it is whether the critical section creates unnecessary contention.
scenario: A high-throughput service synchronizes access to a shared map. As traffic increases, thread contention grows and throughput stops scaling.
investigation: Use thread dumps and profiling to measure monitor contention and time spent inside the critical section. Determine whether the shared state can be partitioned.
resolution: Reduce the critical section, use concurrent data structures where appropriate and partition state by key so independent operations do not share one lock. Do not replace synchronized with another lock without measuring.
prevention: Track lock contention and benchmark with realistic concurrency. Design shared state to minimize contention from the start.

title: GC pauses cause intermittent latency spikes
short: GC tuning starts with understanding allocation and pause behavior; collector flags are not a substitute for profiling.
answer: I would correlate p99 latency with GC events, then profile allocation and object lifetime. I would first reduce unnecessary allocation and only then tune collector and heap settings based on measured behavior.
code: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate object lifetime and choose/tune a collector appropriate to the latency and heap requirements. Avoid changing GC settings blindly.
followups: How do you identify allocation hotspots?
What is a memory leak versus high allocation rate?
mistakes: Increasing heap without analyzing pauses.
Changing collectors without baseline measurements.
interview: I would prove the latency correlation with GC logs and metrics before changing JVM flags.
scenario: A Java service has normal average latency but p99 latency spikes every few minutes. GC logs show long pauses during the same periods.
investigation: Correlate GC pause times with request latency, allocation rate, heap occupancy and old-generation collections. Inspect allocation hotspots with profiling.
resolution: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate object lifetime and choose/tune a collector appropriate to the latency and heap requirements. Avoid changing GC settings blindly.
prevention: Track pause time, allocation rate, heap occupancy and p99 latency together. Load-test with production-like object allocation patterns.

title: A CompletableFuture chain silently stops after an exception
short: CompletableFuture exceptions complete the future exceptionally; they do not automatically behave like synchronous exceptions.
answer: I would inspect the chain for exceptional completion and ensure the final future is observed. I would use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for cleanup, while preserving the failure when recovery is not possible.
code: Make exceptional paths explicit and return a terminal future that callers can observe. Use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for side-effect cleanup/logging.
followups: What happens when an executor rejects a task?
How do you cancel a future chain?
mistakes: Assuming try/catch around submit catches async exceptions.
Ignoring the final future.
interview: Async errors live in the future. If nobody observes the final stage, the business failure can become invisible.
scenario: A multi-step asynchronous workflow produces no final result for some requests. Logs show an exception in an intermediate stage but no response handling.
investigation: Inspect the future chain and exceptional completion paths. Check whether exceptionally/handle/whenComplete is used and whether the final future is awaited.
resolution: Make exceptional paths explicit and return a terminal future that callers can observe. Use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for side-effect cleanup/logging.
prevention: Test both success and failure paths for every asynchronous workflow and propagate correlation IDs through async boundaries.

title: A service leaks ThreadLocal state between requests
short: ThreadLocal values belong to the worker thread, not the request. In pooled executors, the same thread can process many requests.
answer: I would treat ThreadLocal as thread-scoped state and ensure every set has a corresponding remove in a finally block. For request context, I would prefer framework-managed mechanisms when possible. I would also test thread reuse explicitly.
followups: Why can it cause memory leaks?
mistakes: Do not assume a pooled thread is dedicated to one request.
interview: The bug can become both a data-isolation problem and a memory-retention problem.
scenario: A long-running servlet application shows request/user context from one request appearing in a later request handled by the same worker thread.
investigation: Inspect ThreadLocal usage and thread-pool lifecycle. Check whether values are removed in finally blocks and whether pooled threads are reused across requests.
prevention: Set request-scoped context at the boundary and always remove ThreadLocal values in finally. Prefer framework-managed request context where available.

title: CompletableFuture chain silently loses exceptions
short: CompletableFuture failures are stored in the future. They do not automatically become visible to the caller unless the chain is observed or joined.
answer: I would ensure the controller or service returns the composed future or explicitly waits at the correct boundary. Then I would handle failures with exceptionally or handle and log the original cause with correlation context.
followups: How do you add a timeout to a future?
mistakes: Do not ignore a future returned by an important operation.
interview: The interview trap is assuming asynchronous exceptions behave exactly like synchronous exceptions.
scenario: An asynchronous workflow returns a successful HTTP response even though one of the CompletableFuture stages failed.
investigation: Trace the future chain and inspect whether exceptionally/handle/whenComplete or join/get is used. Check whether a failed stage is created but its result is ignored.
prevention: Compose the futures into one returned future, handle exceptions explicitly at the boundary, and avoid launching independent futures whose failures are never observed.

title: JVM GC pauses increase after a traffic increase
short: GC latency is influenced by allocation rate, live-set size and collector behavior, not simply by total heap size.
answer: I would first correlate GC pauses with latency and inspect allocation and promotion rates. Then I would determine whether the issue is excessive allocation, an unexpectedly large live set or collector configuration. I would change one variable at a time and validate with realistic load.
followups: How does G1 work at a high level?
What is a memory leak in Java?
mistakes: Do not equate high heap usage with a GC bug automatically.
interview: Never start by increasing the heap without understanding why the live set or allocation rate changed.
scenario: p99 latency increases because occasional GC pauses grow from tens of milliseconds to over a second after traffic increases.
investigation: Inspect allocation rate, heap occupancy, GC pause times, old-generation promotion and object-retention patterns. Correlate GC events with request latency.
prevention: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate retained objects, choose/tune the collector based on measured behavior, size the heap appropriately and validate changes with production-like load.

title: What is the happens-before relationship in Java?
short: Happens-before defines an ordering that guarantees visibility of one action to another thread.
answer: It is established by synchronization actions such as unlocking then locking the same monitor, volatile writes/read pairs, thread start/join and other concurrency constructs. It is stronger than simply saying one line executed earlier in wall-clock time.
followups: Can instruction reordering break an unsynchronized program?
interview: Happens-before is the JMM visibility and ordering guarantee. I look for an established synchronization edge rather than assuming timing makes a write visible.
scenario: Happens-before defines an ordering that guarantees visibility of one action to another thread.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: Why is double-checked locking safe only with volatile?
short: The singleton reference must be volatile so publication and initialization writes are correctly ordered.
answer: Without volatile, a thread can observe a non-null reference before all constructor writes are visible because publication and initialization can be reordered. Volatile prevents that unsafe publication pattern.
followups: Why is the first null check needed?
Can an enum singleton avoid this complexity?
interview: Double-checked locking needs a volatile instance reference. The volatile write publishes the fully initialized object with the required visibility and ordering guarantees.

title: What is CAS and how is it used in Java concurrency?
short: Compare-and-set atomically changes a value only if it still equals an expected value.
answer: AtomicInteger and many concurrent structures use CAS loops. CAS avoids blocking for some operations, but high contention can cause repeated retries and does not automatically solve multi-variable invariants.
interview: CAS is an optimistic atomic primitive: compare the current value with the expected value and update only when they match. Java atomics build lock-free algorithms from it.

title: What is a lock-free algorithm?
short: A lock-free algorithm guarantees that system-wide progress continues even if individual threads are delayed.
answer: It commonly uses atomic operations such as CAS. Lock-free does not mean wait-free: one thread can still starve while others make progress.
interview: Lock-free means some thread can always make progress. I would use it only when the workload justifies the complexity and after measuring contention.

title: What is the ABA problem?
short: ABA occurs when a value changes from A to B and back to A, making a CAS unable to detect that an intermediate change happened.
answer: Algorithms can use stamped or versioned references to distinguish logically different states that have the same raw value. It matters in non-blocking algorithms and reused nodes.
followups: Can ABA matter in ordinary HashMap code?
interview: The ABA problem is a false assumption that A is unchanged because the current value is A. Version stamps can make the state transition detectable.

title: How does String.intern() work?
short: intern returns a canonical pooled representation of a string.
answer: The JVM maintains a string pool. Interning can reduce duplicate string storage when there are many repeated values, but excessive interning can increase pool pressure and should not be used as a generic performance trick.
followups: Is the string pool on the heap?
interview: intern gives equal strings a shared canonical instance. I use it only when profiling and data characteristics justify it.

title: What is escape analysis in the JVM?
short: Escape analysis lets the JVM determine whether an object or lock escapes a method or thread.
answer: The JIT can use that information for optimizations such as scalar replacement and lock elimination in suitable cases. It is an optimization, so application code should not depend on a specific optimization occurring.
followups: Can all short-lived objects be stack allocated?
interview: Escape analysis can let the JIT eliminate allocations or synchronization when it proves they are unnecessary. I treat it as a runtime optimization and verify with profiling.

title: How does JIT compilation improve Java performance?
short: The JIT compiles frequently executed bytecode into optimized native machine code at runtime.
answer: It uses runtime profiling to optimize hot paths, inline calls, eliminate checks and apply speculative optimizations. Deoptimization can occur when assumptions stop being valid.
interview: Java starts with bytecode execution and the JIT optimizes hot code using runtime information. Warm-up and workload shape therefore matter in benchmarks.

title: What is class initialization order in Java?
short: Class initialization runs static initialization when the class is first actively used.
answer: Superclass initialization precedes subclass initialization, and static fields/blocks execute in textual order within a class. Initialization is synchronized by the JVM so the class is initialized once.
interview: I remember the order as parent class initialization first, then the subclass, with static fields and blocks following source order.

title: How can ClassLoader leaks happen in application servers?
short: A class loader can remain reachable through threads, ThreadLocals, static references or registered callbacks after an application is undeployed.
answer: If the loader cannot be garbage collected, all classes and metadata it loaded may remain reachable, causing metaspace growth across redeployments.
followups: How do you diagnose a classloader leak?
interview: In containers I look for long-lived threads, ThreadLocals, static caches and libraries that retain the application ClassLoader. Cleanup at shutdown is essential.

title: What is the difference between heap and metaspace?
short: Heap stores ordinary Java objects, while metaspace stores class metadata outside the traditional Java heap.
answer: Heap pressure usually manifests as GC and heap OOMs. Metaspace pressure can grow when many classes or class loaders are created, especially in plugin or redeployment scenarios.
interview: Heap and metaspace are different memory areas with different failure symptoms. I check the correct metric before tuning -Xmx or metaspace settings.

title: How do records affect equality and immutability?
short: Records provide concise data carriers with generated accessors, equals, hashCode and toString based on components.
answer: A record is shallowly immutable: its component references are final, but referenced mutable objects can still change. Records are excellent for value-like DTOs and keys.
interview: Records reduce boilerplate for value objects. I still consider defensive copies when a component is a mutable collection or array.

title: What are sealed classes useful for?
short: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend or implement a type.
answer: They make a closed hierarchy explicit and can improve modeling and exhaustiveness in pattern matching. The permitted subclasses must follow the sealing rules.
followups: Can a sealed class have an indirect subclass?
interview: Sealed classes are useful when a domain has a deliberately closed set of variants, such as payment states or command results.

title: What is pattern matching for instanceof?
short: Pattern matching lets an instanceof test declare and bind the matching variable.
answer: It reduces repetitive casts and makes conditional logic clearer. The variable's scope follows the compiler's flow analysis.
interview: It combines the type check and cast, improving readability without changing the underlying object model.

title: What is structured concurrency conceptually?
short: Structured concurrency treats related concurrent tasks as one scoped unit of work.
answer: The parent task controls the lifetime of child tasks, making cancellation, failure propagation and resource management easier to reason about. In Java it is associated with newer concurrency APIs and remains a design concept worth understanding.
followups: How is it different from CompletableFuture?
interview: Structured concurrency makes concurrent subtasks have a clear parent scope, so failures and cancellation can be handled together instead of leaving orphaned work.

title: How does interruption work in Java?
short: Interruption is a cooperative cancellation signal delivered to a thread.
answer: Blocking methods may throw InterruptedException, while code should either propagate it or restore the interrupt flag after handling it. Swallowing interruption can break shutdown and cancellation behavior.
followups: Is interrupt the same as stopping a thread?
interview: I treat interruption as a cancellation request. If I catch InterruptedException and cannot propagate it, I restore the interrupt flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

title: How do you benchmark Java code correctly?
short: Microbenchmarks must account for warm-up, JIT optimization, dead-code elimination and measurement noise.
answer: JMH handles forks, warm-up iterations and measurement infrastructure. For production decisions, microbenchmarks should complement end-to-end profiling rather than replace it.
interview: I use JMH for small JVM benchmarks and real workload tests for service behavior. I never trust a single System.nanoTime loop as a performance conclusion.

title: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iteration?
short: Fail-fast iterators may detect structural modification and throw ConcurrentModificationException, while snapshot or concurrent collections use different semantics.
answer: Fail-fast is a best-effort bug detector, not a thread-safety guarantee. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, while concurrent collections provide their own weakly consistent semantics.
interview: Concurrent iteration semantics depend on the collection. I never use fail-fast behavior as synchronization.

title: What is the difference between AtomicReference and synchronized state?
short: AtomicReference updates one reference atomically without a traditional monitor.
answer: AtomicReference uses CAS-style updates for a single reference. It is useful for lock-free state transitions, but if several fields must change together a monitor or another coordinated design may be clearer.
mistakes: Do not assume atomic reference updates make a multi-step workflow atomic.
interview: I choose AtomicReference when one state reference can be updated atomically. If the invariant spans multiple mutable fields, I prefer a lock or immutable state object swapped as one reference.
